recipes.name: Masa de Nixtamal
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft, cool dough that smells of toasted corn and limestone, with a faint sweetness and a clean mineral finish.
recipes.healthBenefit: Cooking corn with cal frees much of its bound niacin and adds calcium from the lime, which is why masa has fed Mexico for thousands of years, though phytate in the corn still limits how much of that calcium is absorbed.

ingredients.prepNote: white dent corn is the usual choice for tortillas

ingredients.name: cal (food grade slaked lime, calcium hydroxide)
ingredients.prepNote: sold in Mexican markets as cal para nixtamal
for cooking and soaking, drained away afterwards
added while grinding and kneading, a little at a time

instructions: Rinse the dried corn and pick out any broken or dark kernels.
Dissolve the cal in about 250 ml of the water in a large nonreactive pot, then add the rest of the cooking water and the corn and stir; skim off any kernels that float.

Bring to a boil over high heat, then lower to a gentle simmer and cook for 25 to 40 minutes, until a kernel rubbed between your fingers slips its skin and the inside is just tender but still firm at the center.
Take the pot off the heat, cover and leave the corn in its yellow water for 8 to 18 hours, overnight being the usual.
Drain the nixtamal and rinse it lightly, rubbing between your hands to loosen some of the skins; do not wash it clean, as a little of the lime gives masa its flavor and helps it hold together.
Grind the nixtamal in a molino or a hand corn mill, passing it two or three times, adding water a spoonful at a time until the masa is fine and smooth.
Knead the masa for about 5 minutes on the counter, adding water until it feels like soft clay that does not crack at the edges when a ball is pressed flat. It makes about 1.8 kg of masa.
Keep the masa covered with a damp cloth and use it the same day, or wrap it and refrigerate for 1 to 2 days.

Without a mill, mix 500 g masa harina with about 650 to 750 ml warm water and a pinch of salt, knead for 2 to 3 minutes and rest it covered for 15 to 30 minutes; it stands in for fresh masa in any recipe here.

nutritionHighlights.note: Taken up from the cal the corn is cooked and soaked in.
Corn niacin is mostly bound until nixtamalization releases it.
From the whole corn kernel, ground with its germ.

citations.source: México Desconocido, Nixtamal: qué es, cómo se hace (chef Héctor Gil)
Zarela Martínez, Making nixtamal and masa
Rancho Gordo, Making masa from scratch
Hambidge et al., Calcium absorption from tortilla meals, Am J Clin Nutr 2005

recipes.curationNote: Proportions follow Héctor Gil in México Desconocido (1.1 kg corn, 30 g cal, 2 L water, rest 8 to 18 h, grind three times for tortillas) scaled to 1 kg corn, checked against Zarela Martínez and Rancho Gordo for timing. Yield about 1.8 kg masa; one serving is about 100 g of masa, so 18 servings. Cooking water is listed for completeness but drained. Masa harina route added in the last step as the brief asks.

recipes.name: Tortillas de Maíz
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft, warm and lightly freckled from the comal, with a toasty corn smell and a gentle chew.
recipes.healthBenefit: Whole nixtamalized corn gives fiber, calcium and available niacin with no added fat, which makes the tortilla one of the plainer and more nourishing breads there is.

components.note: about 600 g fresh masa

ingredients.prepNote: only as needed to soften the masa

instructions: Knead the masa for a minute, adding water a teaspoon at a time if a pressed ball cracks at the edges; it should feel soft and moist but not sticky.
Divide it into 16 balls of about 35 to 40 g and keep them under a damp cloth.
Heat a comal or heavy skillet over medium to medium high heat for about 5 minutes, until evenly hot, around 400 to 450°F (205 to 230°C) on the surface.
Line a tortilla press with two pieces of plastic cut from a bag, set a ball in the middle and press to a round about 13 cm (5 in) across and 2 to 3 mm thick.
Peel off the top plastic, turn the tortilla onto your hand, peel off the second and lay it on the comal; cook 40 to 45 seconds without moving it, until the edges dry and it releases.
Turn it and cook 60 to 90 seconds, until the underside has brown freckles.
Turn once more for 10 to 15 seconds; press gently with your fingers or a cloth so it puffs, then wrap it in a cloth or tortillero, where the steam keeps the stack soft.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the cal used to make the masa.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Homemade Corn Tortillas
National Park Service, Tumacácori, Tortillas de maíz

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's timings (40 to 45 s, 70 to 90 s, 10 to 15 s and the puff) and 35 to 40 g balls, with fresh masa from the nixtamal base rather than masa harina. NPS Tumacácori confirms the three turns and roughly 2 minutes total. One serving is one tortilla; 16 tortillas use about 600 g masa, six masa servings. No salt, as tortilla masa traditionally has none.

recipes.name: Masa para Tamales
recipes.flavorProfile: Light, fluffy and savory once steamed, rich with lard and seasoned with chicken broth around a soft corn crumb.
recipes.healthBenefit: This is a rich dough: the lard that makes it light also makes each tamal a filling, fat dense food, so tamales sit best beside beans, greens and salsa rather than as an everyday bread.

components.note: about 1 kg fresh masa, coarser grind for tamales
about 250 g, at cool room temperature
about 375 ml, warm

ingredients.prepNote: taste and adjust, the masa should taste a little salty before steaming

instructions: Beat the lard in a stand mixer or with a hand mixer on medium high for 3 to 5 minutes, until it is white and fluffy like whipped cream.
Beat in the baking powder and salt for another 1 to 2 minutes.
With the mixer on medium, add the masa a handful at a time, alternating with splashes of warm broth, until all the masa is in.
Keep beating for 8 to 10 minutes, adding broth until the masa is as soft as thick cake batter that still holds a shape on a spoon.
Drop half a teaspoon of masa into a glass of cold water: if it floats it is ready, and if it sinks beat for 2 to 3 minutes more and test again.
Taste and adjust the salt, then spread about 60 to 70 g on each soaked corn husk or banana leaf and steam the tamales for 60 to 90 minutes, until the masa pulls cleanly away from the wrapper.
With masa harina instead of fresh masa, use 1 kg harina for tamales and 1 to 1.25 L warm broth in the same way.

nutritionHighlights.note: Mostly from the lard beaten into the masa.
Carried in from the nixtamalized corn.

citations.source: Excélsior, Receta masa para tamales básica
Mamá Maggie's Kitchen, Basic Masa for Tamales

recipes.curationNote: Excélsior's proportions (1 kg harina, 250 g lard, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tbsp salt, 1 to 1.25 L broth, 25 tamales, float test) moved onto fresh masa, which needs far less broth. Mamá Maggie's confirms the whipped lard first, alternating additions and the float test. One serving is the masa for one tamal, about 60 to 70 g.

recipes.name: Tortillas de Harina
recipes.flavorProfile: Thin, soft and pliable with toasted spots, tasting of wheat and a little lard, and tearing in tender layers.
recipes.healthBenefit: Made with refined flour and lard, these are a richer, plainer bread than corn tortillas, best eaten as the wrapper for beans, meat and vegetables.

components.note: about 90 g, soft

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.prepNote: hot to the touch, about 120 to 130°F (50 to 55°C)

instructions: Mix the flour and salt in a wide bowl, then rub in the lard with your fingertips until the flour feels like damp sand, 2 to 3 minutes.
Pour in the hot water a little at a time, mixing with your hand until a soft dough forms, then knead on the counter for 3 to 5 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Divide into 16 balls of about 55 g, cover with a cloth and rest for 15 to 20 minutes so the gluten relaxes.
Heat a comal or griddle over medium high heat for 5 minutes, to about 450 to 500°F (230 to 260°C) on the surface.
Roll each ball with a palote (thin rolling pin) into a round 23 to 25 cm (9 to 10 in) across and as thin as you can manage, turning it a quarter turn between strokes.
Cook 20 to 30 seconds, until bubbles rise, turn and cook 20 to 30 seconds more, pressing any big bubbles down with a cloth so they brown in spots.
Stack them in a cloth as they come off the comal to keep them soft.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the lard worked into the dough.

citations.source: Food My Muse, Sonoran Tortillas de Harina
National Park Service, Tumacácori, Tortillas de harina

recipes.curationNote: Food My Muse (raised in Sonora) gives 4 cups flour, 1/3 cup lard, hot water, rest 15 to 20 min and a hot comal; NPS Tumacácori gives the older ranch ratio (2 lb flour to 1/2 lb lard) and the thin Sonoran style. Lard set between the two at about 18% of flour. One serving is one tortilla. The giant sobaquera style is mentioned by NPS but this keeps a home size.

recipes.name: Totopos
recipes.flavorProfile: Crisp, salty corn chips that shatter cleanly and taste of toasted masa, made for scooping salsa and beans.
recipes.healthBenefit: Fried totopos absorb oil and are a snack to enjoy in modest handfuls; baking them instead keeps the corn fiber and calcium with much less fat.

components.note: a day old or left out to dry

ingredients.prepNote: about what the chips absorb from 500 to 750 ml heated for frying

instructions: Spread the tortillas on the counter for 30 minutes to 2 hours so they dry a little, which makes them crisp rather than chewy.
Stack them and cut each into 6 wedges.
Heat 2 to 3 cm (about 1 in) of oil in a heavy pan to 350 to 365°F (175 to 185°C).
Fry the wedges in batches for 1 to 2 minutes, turning, until golden and the bubbling slows; do not let them go dark or they turn bitter.
Lift them onto paper towels and salt them while hot.
To bake instead, brush the wedges lightly with oil and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 15 to 25 minutes, turning once, until crisp.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the frying oil the chips take up.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, How to make tostadas and chips at home
Directo al Paladar, Cómo hacer totopos caseros

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's drying step and frying guidance, with her 350°F baking alternative; Directo al Paladar confirms frying until golden and draining. Fat listed is the amount absorbed, not the frying bath. One serving is 12 chips (two tortillas).

recipes.name: Tostadas (Shells)
recipes.flavorProfile: A flat, golden, crackling corn disc with a toasted flavor, sturdy enough to hold beans, meat and salsa.
recipes.healthBenefit: A fried tostada carries some oil, while a baked or comal toasted one keeps the plain nutrition of the corn tortilla with almost none.

components.note: left out to dry

ingredients.prepNote: about what 12 tortillas absorb from a pan with 1 cm of oil

instructions: Lay the tortillas out on the counter or a tray for 30 minutes to a couple of hours so they dry slightly.
Heat about 1 cm (1/2 in) of oil in a skillet over medium heat for 4 to 6 minutes, to about 350°F (175°C), hot but not smoking.
Fry one tortilla at a time for 45 seconds to 1 minute per side, until golden and rigid, pressing it flat with a spatula.
Drain upright in a tall strainer or flat on paper towels; they crisp further as they cool.
To bake instead, set them on a baking sheet at 350°F (175°C) for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, or toast them on a dry comal over medium heat, turning often, until crisp.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, How to make tostadas and chips at home
Directo al Paladar, Cómo hacer totopos caseros

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's method in full (dry, 1/2 in oil, 45 s to 1 min a side, or 350°F for 25 to 30 min, or comal). Directo al Paladar was compared for the fried crisp and draining. Only one dedicated tostada source opened fully; other search results were US blogs, so not used. One serving is one tostada.

recipes.name: Bolillo
recipes.flavorProfile: A thin, crackling golden crust around a soft, airy white crumb, mildly salty and made for tortas and molletes.
recipes.healthBenefit: A plain white bread roll: mostly refined wheat carbohydrate, best paired with beans, eggs or vegetables to round out a meal.

components.note: about 40 g, soft

ingredients.baseName: Grains, wheat flour, white, bread flour

instructions: Heap the flour on the counter or in a bowl and make a well; put the yeast and 120 ml of the lukewarm water in the center and leave it 5 to 10 minutes, until foamy.
Draw in the flour with the remaining water, then add the sugar and salt and mix to a rough dough.
Work in the lard and knead for 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, elastic and comes cleanly off the counter.
Cover and let it rise in a warm place until doubled, 45 to 90 minutes.
Punch it down and divide into 10 pieces of about 85 g; flatten each, fold the edges to the center, then roll it into a spindle with tapered ends, pressing the ends into points.
Set them on a lined baking sheet, cover and let rise until nearly doubled, 40 to 60 minutes.
Heat the oven to 450 to 480°F (230 to 250°C) with an empty tray on the lowest rack.
Cut a slash about 1 cm deep along the length of each roll, slide them in and pour a cup of hot water into the empty tray for steam.
Bake for 15 to 20 minutes, until golden and hollow sounding when tapped underneath, then cool on a rack before cutting.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the gluten in bread flour.

citations.source: México Desconocido, Cómo hacer bolillos
Grupo Animal, Bolillo, pan mexicano

recipes.curationNote: México Desconocido's recipe (500 g flour, yeast in a well with water, 10 min knead, rise to double, 10 rolls, 250°C with a water tray for crust) and Grupo Animal's (rise 45 to 90 min, 220°C about 20 min, slash along the length). Lard used as the fat, which bakers prefer and México Desconocido allows (it lists manteca vegetal or oil). Salt reduced from the source's 2 tablespoons, which reads as an error, to 2% of flour.

recipes.name: Telera
recipes.flavorProfile: A soft, flat, lightly sweet roll with a thin golden crust and two pressed lines, made to be split for tortas.
recipes.healthBenefit: A plain enriched white roll that carries the beans, meat and vegetables of a torta, and is mostly refined carbohydrate by itself.

components.note: about 25 g, melted

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

instructions: Stir the yeast and sugar into the lukewarm water and leave it a few minutes, until bubbly.
Add the flour, melted lard and salt and mix on low with a dough hook for 1 to 2 minutes, then knead on medium for about 8 minutes (or 10 minutes by hand) until smooth and elastic.
Oil the bowl, cover and let rise in a warm place until doubled, about 1 hour; for more flavor, refrigerate overnight and bring back to room temperature for about 2 hours.
Press the dough down, divide into 6 pieces, roll into balls, dust with flour and rest covered for 15 minutes.
Flatten each ball into an oval about 13 by 8 cm (5 by 3 in) on a lined baking sheet.
Press a floured wooden spoon handle deep into each oval twice along its length, almost through the dough, to make the three sections.
Dust lightly with flour, cover and let rise about 30 minutes, until almost doubled, while the oven heats to 400°F (200°C).
Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, until golden, and cool slightly before splitting.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the wheat flour and a little sugar.

citations.source: Rick Bayless, Teleras
Camila Made, Teleras

recipes.curationNote: Rick Bayless's recipe followed closely (420 g flour, 25 g lard or oil, 2 tbsp sugar, 6 rolls, two deep presses, 400°F 18 to 20 min); Camila Made's version agrees in every measure and was used to confirm. Lard chosen over the oil alternative.

recipes.name: Salsa Roja Asada
recipes.flavorProfile: Smoky, chunky and bright, with charred tomato sweetness, a sharp serrano bite and roasted garlic underneath.
recipes.healthBenefit: A fresh vegetable salsa with almost no fat, bringing vitamin C and the red carotenoids of tomato to whatever it tops.

ingredients.cutPrep: whole, about 4, stems removed after roasting
coarse salt if you have it

instructions: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat and lay on the tomatoes, serranos, onion and garlic.
Roast, turning with tongs, until blistered and blackened in patches and soft: 4 to 6 minutes for the garlic and chiles, 8 to 12 minutes for the tomatoes and onion.
Peel the garlic, pull the stems off the chiles and chop the onion.
In a molcajete, grind the garlic with the salt to a paste, then add the chiles and grind until broken down.
Add the onion, then the tomatoes with their charred skins, and grind to a coarse, juicy salsa.
Stir in the cilantro and taste for salt; it should taste a little salty by itself. It keeps 3 days in the refrigerator.

citations.source: Mexican Food Journal, Salsa Molcajeteada
Martín Gerardo Ramírez Correa (Jalisco and Guanajuato), Salsa asada de jitomate y serrano, Cookpad

recipes.curationNote: Mexican Food Journal's molcajete order (garlic to a paste, onion, then tomatoes, salt so it tastes salty by itself, keeps 3 days) with the Ramírez Correa family's all tomato and serrano proportions from Los Altos de Jalisco (4 large tomatoes, 6 serranos, onion, 2 garlic, roasted on a low comal about 10 minutes). Tomatillos from the Journal version left out so this stays the red roasted table salsa. One serving is 2 tablespoons; the batch is about 2 1/2 cups.

recipes.name: Salsa Verde Cocida
recipes.flavorProfile: Tangy and smooth with a fresh cilantro lift and steady serrano heat, deepened and rounded by a short fry in hot oil.
recipes.healthBenefit: Tomatillos, chile and cilantro make a light sauce with vitamin C and a little fiber, and only a spoonful of oil for the whole batch.

ingredients.cutPrep: about 1 cup leaves and upper stems

instructions: Put the tomatillos, serranos and garlic in a pot, cover with water and bring to a boil over high heat.
Lower to medium and simmer for 8 to 12 minutes, just until the tomatillos turn from bright to olive green and soften without bursting; lift them out and keep 120 ml of the water.
Blend the tomatillos, chiles and garlic with the reserved water until smooth, then add the onion, cilantro and salt and blend again; taste for heat and salt.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat until hot but not smoking, pour in the salsa (it will spatter) and bring it to a boil.
Simmer for 6 to 7 minutes, until it darkens a shade and thickens slightly.
Cool and keep it covered in the refrigerator for up to 1 week; the heat mellows as it sits.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Cooked Salsa Verde
Federico Negrete (Ciudad de México), Salsa Verde, Cookpad
Grupo Animal, Cómo hacer salsa verde

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's proportions and the fry in oil for 6 to 7 minutes; Federico Negrete's Mexico City home version and Grupo Animal both confirm boiling until the color changes and blending with raw cilantro and onion; Grupo Animal adds the warning not to let the tomatillos burst. One serving is 2 tablespoons; the batch is about 2 1/2 cups.

recipes.name: Salsa Verde Cruda
recipes.flavorProfile: Sharp, grassy and cool, the raw tomatillo tartness softened into a pale, creamy green by avocado.
recipes.healthBenefit: Raw tomatillo keeps its vitamin C, and the avocado adds monounsaturated fat and potassium to a taco without any cooking oil.
instructions: Put the tomatillos, onion, garlic, half the serrano and the salt in a blender and blend until smooth, adding a spoonful or two of water only if the blades stall.
Add the avocado and cilantro and blend again until pale green and creamy.
Taste and blend in more serrano for more heat and more salt if needed.
Serve within a few hours; to keep it, press plastic wrap onto the surface and refrigerate for up to 1 day, stirring before serving.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the raw tomatillos and chile.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Raw Salsa Verde with Avocado
Grupo Animal, Cómo hacer salsa verde (cruda y cremosa con aguacate)

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's quantities (1 lb tomatillos, 1 avocado, 2 tbsp onion, 1/4 cup cilantro, half the chile first), with Grupo Animal's raw and avocado versions for the garlic and the order of blending the avocado in last. One serving is 2 tablespoons; the batch is about 2 cups.

recipes.name: Pico de Gallo
recipes.flavorProfile: Crunchy, juicy and fresh, with ripe tomato, sharp white onion, green serrano heat and a squeeze of lime.
recipes.healthBenefit: Raw tomato, onion, chile, cilantro and lime make a fat free relish that brings vitamin C and a little fiber to any plate.

ingredients.cutPrep: 4 Roma (saladet) tomatoes, in small even dice
half a white onion, in small dice

ingredients.prepNote: seeds and veins removed for milder heat

instructions: Halve the tomatoes and scoop out most of the seeds if you want a drier, crisper salsa, then cut them into small, even cubes.
Dice the onion to the same size and finely chop the serranos and cilantro.
If making it ahead, soak the chopped onion in ice water for 10 minutes and drain it well to soften its bite.
Mix everything in a glass or ceramic bowl, add the lime juice and salt and stir gently.
Let it sit at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes before serving so the flavors come together.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the tomato, serrano and lime.

citations.source: Excélsior, Pico de gallo tradicional
Directo al Paladar, Cómo hacer pico de gallo

recipes.curationNote: Excélsior's quantities (4 saladet, half an onion, 2 to 3 serranos, half a bunch cilantro, 2 to 3 tbsp lime) and its rest and onion soak tips; Directo al Paladar agrees on the classic five ingredients and serrano first. One serving is 1/4 cup; the batch is about 2 1/2 cups.

recipes.name: Salsa Taquera de Chile de Árbol
recipes.flavorProfile: Thin, brick red and fiercely hot, with toasted chile de árbol, a tart tomatillo edge and charred garlic.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very hot, very light salsa made mostly of vegetables and dried chile, meant to be used by the spoonful.
instructions: Heat a dry comal over medium heat and roast the tomatillos, tomato, onion and garlic, turning, until blackened in spots and soft, 8 to 12 minutes.
Pass the chiles de árbol over the comal for only 10 to 20 seconds a side, until fragrant and a shade darker; burnt chiles make the salsa bitter.
Peel the garlic and blend the chiles with the salt and half the water first, until the chile is finely broken up.
Add the onion, garlic, tomato and tomatillos and the rest of the water and blend briefly, leaving some texture; the salsa should be thin and pourable.
Taste for salt, and if the tomatillos are sharp, add a pinch of sugar. It keeps 5 days in the refrigerator.

citations.source: Grupo Animal, Salsa taquera: recetas tradicionales para roja y verde
Mexican Food Journal, Salsa Taquera (Salsa de Chile de Árbol)

recipes.curationNote: Grupo Animal's roasted salsa roja de árbol (10 to 15 árbol chiles barely toasted, chiles blended with salt first, pulse for texture) with tomatillo added as the base description asks and as many taquerías do. Mexican Food Journal's oil emulsified version was compared and its oil left out to keep the thin taquería style. Árbol chiles weigh about 0.4 g each. One serving is 2 tablespoons; the batch is about 2 cups.

recipes.name: Salsa Macha
recipes.flavorProfile: A deep red chile oil, crunchy with peanuts and seeds, smoky from morita and sharp from árbol, with fried garlic sweetness.
recipes.healthBenefit: This is an oil condiment and rich by the spoonful, though the peanuts and seeds bring protein, vitamin E and minerals with the fat.

ingredients.prepNote: any neutral seed oil; some Veracruz cooks use part olive oil

instructions: Warm the oil in a skillet over very low heat, to about 250 to 275°F (120 to 135°C); it should only shimmer, never smoke.
Fry the garlic for 2 to 3 minutes, until pale gold, and lift it out.
Fry the chiles for 20 to 40 seconds, just until they puff and darken a shade, and lift them out before they burn.
Fry the peanuts for 2 to 3 minutes, then the pumpkin seeds and sesame for 1 to 2 minutes more, until the seeds pop and smell toasted.
Take the pan off the heat and let everything cool for 10 to 15 minutes.
Pulse the chiles, garlic, nuts and seeds with the salt and some of the oil in a blender to a coarse crumb, then stir in the rest of the oil.
Keep it in a sterilized jar with the solids covered by oil, in a cool place or the refrigerator, for up to 1 month.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the seed oil, peanuts and seeds.
From the pumpkin and sesame seeds.
Mostly from the oil, which is most of the jar.

citations.source: Excélsior, Receta de salsa macha tradicional
Food and Pleasure, Salsa macha (versión clásica veracruzana)

recipes.curationNote: Excélsior's recipe followed for quantities and frying order (garlic, chiles, peanuts, then seeds, very low heat, about 1/2 liter). Food and Pleasure confirms the Veracruz classic of morita, árbol, peanuts, sesame and garlic. Storage set at 1 month as a careful middle between the sources' ranges. One serving is 1 tablespoon.

recipes.name: Salsa Ranchera
recipes.flavorProfile: A warm, brothy tomato sauce with fresh serrano heat, a little garlic and onion, and a hint of thyme, made to be spooned over eggs.
recipes.healthBenefit: Mostly cooked tomato with a spoonful of oil, it brings lycopene and vitamin C and keeps the eggs it covers a light breakfast.
instructions: Roast the tomatoes, serranos and garlic on a dry comal over medium heat, turning, until soft and blistered, 8 to 12 minutes; do not burn the garlic.
Peel the garlic and stem the chiles, then blend them with the tomatoes, onion, thyme and water until fairly smooth, about 1 minute.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium high heat until it shimmers and pour in the sauce carefully, as it spatters.
Season with salt and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until it turns deep red and thickens slightly but stays brothy; loosen with a little water if needed.
Stir in the cilantro and cook 1 minute more, then keep it warm while the eggs are fried. It keeps 4 days in the refrigerator.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the cooked tomatoes, more available after cooking with oil.

citations.source: Mexican Food Journal, Huevos Rancheros (Salsa Ranchera)
La Opinión, Cómo hacer fácil y bien una salsa ranchera mexicana

recipes.curationNote: Mexican Food Journal's blend and fry with thyme, simmered about 10 minutes, doubled; La Opinión's roasting of tomatoes, chiles and garlic first and cilantro in the last minute. One serving is 1/2 cup, enough for one plate of huevos rancheros.

recipes.name: Chiltomate
recipes.flavorProfile: Chunky and smoky, with sweet charred tomato, fragrant habanero heat and a fresh hit of cilantro.
recipes.healthBenefit: Charred tomato and a little habanero make a fat free sauce with vitamin C and the red carotenoids of tomato.

ingredients.cutPrep: a quarter of a white onion

ingredients.name: habanero chile
ingredients.prepNote: add half, then more to taste

ingredients.cutPrep: about 1 cup coarsely chopped leaves and upper stems

instructions: Heat a dry comal over medium heat and char the tomatoes, onion and habanero, turning once, until blackened in patches and soft, 10 to 12 minutes; or broil them on a sheet for the same time.
Let them cool a little, then chop the onion and seed and chop the habanero, keeping your face away from its fumes.
Mash the tomatoes completely in a molcajete, then work in the onion, cilantro and salt.
Add half the habanero, mash it in and taste, adding more for more heat.
Serve warm or at room temperature; in a blender, pulse just until combined and still chunky.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Basic Yucatecan Tomato Sauce (Salsa de Chiltomate)
México Desconocido, Salsa de chiltomate

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's quantities and molcajete method (1 lb tomatoes, a quarter onion, 1 habanero, 1 cup cilantro, 10 to 12 min on the comal); México Desconocido confirms roasting all three and grinding together, with up to 4 or 5 habaneros for the hotter Yucatecan table. One serving is 1/4 cup; the batch is about 2 cups.

recipes.name: Guacamole
recipes.flavorProfile: Creamy and chunky, with buttery avocado lifted by a pounded paste of onion, serrano and cilantro, lime and coarse salt.
recipes.healthBenefit: Avocado brings monounsaturated fat, fiber and potassium, so guacamole is a rich but nourishing topping in place of cheese or cream.
instructions: In a molcajete, grind half the onion, the serrano, half the cilantro and the salt to a rough paste, 1 to 2 minutes.
Scoop in the avocado and mash it into the paste with the pestle or a fork, leaving some chunks.
Fold in the rest of the onion and cilantro and half the lime juice, then taste and add more lime and salt as needed.
Serve right away in the molcajete; to hold it up to 2 hours, press plastic wrap onto its surface.

citations.source: Maricruz Avalos, Authentic Guacamole Recipe in a Molcajete
Riu Palace Cabo San Lucas (chef Edilson Rodríguez Soto), Prepara el auténtico guacamole

recipes.curationNote: Maricruz Avalos's molcajete method (aromatics ground to a paste with salt first, avocado mashed in, lime to taste) and Chef Rodríguez Soto's chunky texture and early lime. Tomato, garlic and cumin from Avalos left out to keep the plain central Mexican version the base describes. One serving is 1/4 cup; the batch is about 2 cups.

recipes.name: Manteca (Rendered Lard)
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft, creamy and mild, with a gentle roasted pork flavor that makes beans, tamales and flour tortillas taste the way they do at home.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lard is pure fat and rich, used by the spoonful; it is mostly monounsaturated and saturated fat, and home rendered lard carries none of the trans fat of hydrogenated shortening.

ingredients.cutPrep: fresh back fat or leaf fat, skin removed, in 1 to 2 cm cubes
ingredients.prepNote: chilled or half frozen so it cuts cleanly
keeps the fat from sticking at the start; it cooks off

instructions: Cut the chilled fat into small, even cubes, or ask the butcher to grind it, so it melts evenly.
Put the fat and water in a heavy pot or cazo over low heat, about 225 to 250°F (105 to 120°C) in the fat once it melts.
Cook uncovered for 45 minutes to 1 1/2 hours, stirring every 5 to 10 minutes, as the water cooks off and the fat melts and the pieces shrink and turn golden.
When the bubbling slows and the pieces are crisp and golden, take the pot off the heat before anything browns darkly; scorched lard tastes bitter.
Ladle the liquid fat through a fine strainer lined with cheesecloth into clean, heatproof glass jars, and keep the crisp pieces (chicharrón) for tacos or beans.
Let the lard cool uncovered; it turns from clear yellow to white and firm. Cover and refrigerate for up to 3 months, or freeze for longer.

nutritionHighlights.note: Oleic acid is the largest share of the fat in lard.
About two fifths of the fat, so it is used in measured spoonfuls.
Small amounts in lard from pigs raised outdoors.

citations.source: Directo al Paladar (Pakus), Cómo hacer manteca de cerdo casera
México Desconocido, La manteca, la injusta salida de su uso en la cocina tradicional

recipes.curationNote: No Mexican step by step rendering recipe could be opened; the method follows Directo al Paladar (small cubes, a splash of water, low heat about 45 minutes, strain through cheesecloth, cools from yellow to white), which is the same wet rendering used in Mexican kitchens, and México Desconocido gives its place in tamales, refritos and carnitas. 1 kg of back fat gives roughly 700 g of lard. One serving is 1 tablespoon, about 14 g, so the batch is about 50 servings. The nutrients read from the raw back fat include the chicharrón that is strained out, so the fat per serving reads somewhat high.

recipes.name: Caldo de Pollo (Chicken Stock)
recipes.flavorProfile: Clear, golden and savory, with sweet onion and carrot, a little garlic and the herbal warmth of thyme, marjoram and bay.
recipes.healthBenefit: A light, warming stock that brings some protein, gelatin from the feet and backs, and the minerals of the vegetables to rice, soups and sauces.

ingredients.baseName: Chicken, broiler, back, meat and skin
ingredients.prepNote: or one 1.5 kg whole chicken in pieces

instructions: Put the chicken and feet in a large pot with the cold water and bring to a boil over high heat.
Lower the heat to medium low and skim off the gray foam for the first 5 to 10 minutes.
Add the onion, garlic, carrot, celery, parsley, thyme, marjoram, bay leaves, peppercorns and salt.
Simmer gently, partly covered, for 1 to 1 1/2 hours; if using a whole chicken, lift out the breasts after 30 minutes and the thighs after 50 minutes to shred for other dishes.
Strain the stock through a fine sieve and discard the bones and vegetables.
Cool it quickly, refrigerate, and lift off the fat once it sets. It keeps 4 to 5 days in the refrigerator or 3 months frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: Some protein and gelatin from the backs and feet.
From the onion, carrot and celery.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Mexican Chicken Broth (Caldo de Pollo)
Zarela Martínez, Chicken Stock (Caldo de Pollo)

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich's herbs (thyme, marjoram, bay, parsley, peppercorns) and water to chicken ratio, with Zarela Martínez's wings and backs option, short gentle simmer and storage times. Chicken feet added as Mexican markets sell them for caldo. About 3 liters strained; one serving is 1 cup (250 ml), 12 servings. The nutrients read from the whole chicken and vegetables, which are strained out, so protein and fat per cup read higher than the clear broth carries.

recipes.name: Pollo Deshebrado (Shredded Chicken)
recipes.flavorProfile: Tender, moist strands of chicken lightly seasoned with onion, garlic and bay, ready to fill tacos, flautas, tostadas and tamales.
recipes.healthBenefit: Poached breast is lean, high quality protein with very little added fat, a light filling for many Mexican dishes.

ingredients.baseName: Chicken, broiler, breast, skinless, boneless, meat
ingredients.cutPrep: bone in breasts or boneless, skinless
ingredients.prepNote: thighs may replace part of it for juicier meat

ingredients.cutPrep: cold, enough to cover by 3 cm
ingredients.prepNote: the poaching liquid is a light broth to keep

instructions: Put the chicken, onion, garlic, bay leaf and salt in a pot and cover with cold water by about 3 cm.
Bring to a boil over medium high heat, skim the foam, then lower to a gentle simmer.
Simmer 20 to 25 minutes for boneless breasts or 30 to 35 minutes for bone in, until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Turn off the heat and let the chicken cool in the broth for 15 minutes so it stays moist.
Lift it out, pull off any skin and bones, and shred it along the grain with two forks or your fingers.
Moisten the shredded chicken with a few spoonfuls of the broth. It keeps 3 days in the refrigerator or 3 months frozen.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Mexican Chicken Broth (Caldo de Pollo), which yields shredded chicken
Elishita, Pollo deshebrado con verduras, Cookpad México

recipes.curationNote: The home method both sources use: chicken simmered with garlic, onion and salt, then shredded, with the broth kept. Pati Jinich's broth page gives cooling the chicken in the broth and shredding without skin and bone. Kept as its own recipe, not a component of Caldo de Pollo, so dishes can call for either without a loop. 1 kg raw breast gives about 4 cups shredded; one serving is 1/2 cup.

recipes.name: Frijoles de la Olla
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft, creamy beans in a dark, savory broth, scented with onion, garlic and the resinous bite of epazote.
recipes.healthBenefit: Beans bring plant protein, a lot of fiber, folate, iron and magnesium, and only a spoonful of lard for the whole pot.

components.note: 3 tablespoons, cooked in with the beans

ingredients.prepNote: bayo, flor de mayo or black beans are cooked the same way
cilantro in the north, where epazote is not used
added only once the beans are soft

instructions: Spread the beans on a tray, pick out stones and broken beans, and rinse them well; soaking overnight in cold water shortens the cooking but is optional.
Put the beans, onion, garlic, lard and 2 1/2 liters of the water in a clay pot or heavy pot and bring to a boil over medium high heat.
Lower to a gentle simmer and cook partly covered for 2 to 3 hours, adding hot water whenever the broth drops below the beans; cold water toughens them.
When a bean crushes easily between your fingers, add the salt and the epazote and simmer uncovered for 5 to 10 minutes more.
Serve in bowls with plenty of broth. They keep 5 days in the refrigerator; in a pressure cooker, cook 30 to 35 minutes once it hisses, then salt and boil 5 minutes.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the beans, which pair with corn tortillas.

citations.source: El Universal Menú, Cómo hacer frijoles de la olla
Grupo Animal, Cómo hacer frijoles refritos (cooking the beans first)

recipes.curationNote: El Universal's quantities (1/2 kg beans, 2 sprigs epazote, onion, 2 garlic, 3 tbsp lard, 3 L water) and both its clay pot (2 to 3 hours, hot water, salt at the end) and pressure cooker times; Grupo Animal for picking and rinsing and the test of a bean that crushes when pressed. Pinto beans stand in the database for bayo and flor de mayo, which are not listed. Onion reduced from 2 cups to one onion. 500 g dry beans gives about 8 cups with broth; one serving is 1 cup.

recipes.name: Frijoles Refritos
recipes.flavorProfile: Thick, creamy and savory, the beans mashed into hot lard until glossy, with a whisper of fried onion and chile.
recipes.healthBenefit: Still a good source of fiber, folate and plant protein, though richer than beans from the pot because of the lard they are fried in.

components.note: about 4 cups beans with some of their broth
4 tablespoons for frying

ingredients.cutPrep: a thick chunk of white onion

ingredients.prepNote: optional, removed before mashing; some cooks use dried chiles de árbol
to taste, the beans are already salted

instructions: Heat the lard in a wide, heavy skillet over medium high heat until it shimmers, about 350°F (175°C).
Fry the onion and serrano for 2 to 3 minutes, until the onion browns at the edges, then lift them out.
Add the beans with some of their broth, carefully as they spatter, and let them come to a boil.
Mash them in the pan with a bean masher, adding broth a splash at a time, until thick and creamy, 5 to 10 minutes.
Keep cooking and stirring over medium heat until the beans pull away from the pan and are as thick as you like; taste for salt.
Serve hot; they thicken as they cool and can be loosened with broth or water when reheated. They keep 4 days in the refrigerator.

nutritionHighlights.note: Mostly from the lard used to fry them.

citations.source: Abraham Jauregui (Guadalajara, Jalisco), Frijoles refritos con manteca de puerco, Cookpad
Grupo Animal, Cómo hacer frijoles refritos

recipes.curationNote: Grupo Animal's method (onion and serrano fried in plenty of hot lard, beans mashed in the pan until thick and creamy) with Abraham Jauregui's Guadalajara amount of about 5 tablespoons lard for 6 servings, set here at 4. Jauregui also fries garlic, chiles de árbol and torn tortillas in the lard; those are left as a variation. One serving is 1/2 cup; the batch is about 3 cups.

recipes.name: Arroz Rojo (Mexican Red Rice)
recipes.flavorProfile: Fluffy, separate grains tinted orange red, tasting of fried rice, sweet tomato and chicken stock, with bits of carrot and pea.
recipes.healthBenefit: A comforting starch side with some vitamin A from the carrot and tomato, cooked in stock with only a little oil.

components.note: 2 cups, hot

ingredients.cutPrep: 1 cup long grain (Morelos style), rinsed until clear and dried
a quarter of a white onion

ingredients.prepNote: laid on top, removed before serving
to taste, depending on the stock

instructions: Rinse the rice under cold water, rubbing gently, until the water runs clear, then drain and let it dry completely, 15 to 30 minutes.
Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic into a thick purée.
Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium high heat and fry the dry rice, stirring constantly, until the grains turn opaque and lightly golden, 5 to 7 minutes.
Pour in the purée and stir over medium heat until the rice absorbs it and the pan looks almost dry, 3 to 4 minutes.
Add the hot stock, salt, carrot and peas, stir once, lay the serrano on top and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat to the minimum and cook for 15 minutes without stirring.
Fluff gently from the edges toward the center with a fork, cover and cook 3 minutes more, then rest off the heat, covered, for 10 minutes before serving.

citations.source: México Desconocido, Arroz rojo, receta de la abuela
Grupo Animal, La receta de la abuela para hacer arroz rojo mexicano
Camila Made, Arroz a la Mexicana

recipes.curationNote: Both México Desconocido and Grupo Animal give the same grandmother's recipe (1 cup rice, 2 cups stock, 2 tomatoes, a quarter onion, garlic, carrot, a whole serrano, optional peas) with the 15 minute covered cook, fluff and 10 minute rest; Camila Made adds frying until milky white and the oil amount. One serving is 3/4 cup; the batch is about 3 cups.

recipes.name: Arroz Blanco (Mexican White Rice)
recipes.flavorProfile: Light, fluffy and savory, with the toasty taste of fried rice and a mild onion and garlic stock.
recipes.healthBenefit: A plain starch side, cooked in stock with a little oil, that pairs with beans for a fuller protein and fiber plate.

components.note: 2 cups, blended with the onion and garlic

ingredients.cutPrep: 1 cup long grain, rinsed until clear and dried

ingredients.prepNote: to taste, depending on the stock

instructions: Rinse the rice in cold water several times until the water runs almost clear, then drain well and let it dry.
Blend the stock with the onion and garlic until smooth.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and fry the rice, stirring, until the grains turn opaque and just begin to color, 4 to 6 minutes.
Pour in the blended stock, add the salt and the drops of lime, stir gently once and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover, lower the heat to the minimum and cook 15 to 20 minutes without stirring, until the liquid is absorbed.
Turn off the heat, rest covered for 5 to 10 minutes, and fluff with a fork before serving.

citations.source: Excélsior, Cómo hacer arroz blanco: el truco para que quede lleno de sabor
Codiego, Arroz blanco, Cookpad México

recipes.curationNote: Excélsior's recipe (1 cup rice, 2 cups chicken stock blended with onion and garlic, 2 tbsp oil, 15 to 20 minutes covered) with Codiego's frying until the grains separate. Excélsior's 1 tablespoon of salt reduced because the stock is salted. The drops of lime are a common Mexican home habit and optional. One serving is 3/4 cup; the batch is about 3 cups.

recipes.name: Arroz Verde (Green Rice with Poblano)
recipes.flavorProfile: Bright green and fragrant, with mild poblano heat, plenty of cilantro and sweet corn kernels through the fluffy rice.
recipes.healthBenefit: Poblano and cilantro add vitamin C and green carotenoids to a rice side, and corn adds a little fiber.

components.note: 1 3/4 cups, hot

ingredients.cutPrep: 1 cup long grain, soaked 5 minutes, rinsed and drained

ingredients.name: poblano chiles
ingredients.cutPrep: stemmed, seeded and veined, in pieces

ingredients.prepNote: vegetable oil, or butter in Puebla homes
to taste, depending on the stock

instructions: Soak the rice in warm water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse with cold water and drain well.
Blend the poblanos, cilantro, onion, garlic and water until completely smooth.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium high heat until it shimmers and fry the rice, stirring constantly, until the grains turn milky white, 3 to 4 minutes.
Stir in the corn and toast it with the rice for 1 minute.
Pour in the green purée, lower the heat to medium low and stir until the rice has absorbed it, 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the hot stock and salt, bring to a boil, then cover, lower the heat and cook 15 minutes.
Fluff gently, cover and cook 5 minutes more, then rest off the heat and fluff again before serving.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the raw blended poblano and cilantro.

citations.source: Camila Made, Arroz Verde (Mexican Green Rice)
Excélsior, Arroz verde poblano

recipes.curationNote: Camila Made's method and amounts (1 cup rice, 2 poblanos, a bunch of cilantro, onion, garlic, corn from 1 ear, 1 3/4 cups stock, fry until milky white, 15 plus 5 minutes) and Excélsior's Puebla style arroz poblano, which confirms the same blend and the corn and uses butter as the fat. Oil reduced from 4 to 3 tablespoons. Poblano is not in the database and is not counted in nutrients. One serving is 3/4 cup; the batch is about 3 1/2 cups.

recipes.name: Salsa de Guajillo
recipes.flavorProfile: Brick red, smooth and mildly hot, with the fruity, slightly tangy taste of guajillo, softened by tomato, garlic and a touch of cumin and oregano.
recipes.healthBenefit: Dried chiles and tomato bring vitamin A carotenoids and vitamin C to a sauce that uses only a little oil.

ingredients.prepNote: the soaking and cooking water, part of it blended in

instructions: Heat a comal or heavy skillet over medium low heat and toast the chiles a few seconds per side, pressing them flat, just until fragrant and blistered; they turn bitter if they scorch.
Put the chiles in a pot with the tomatoes, onion and garlic, cover with the water, bring to a boil, then turn off the heat and let the chiles soak 15 minutes until soft.
Blend the chiles, tomatoes, onion and garlic with the cumin, oregano and about 2 cups of the soaking water until completely smooth, 1 to 2 minutes.
Pour through a fine strainer, pressing with a spoon, and discard the bits of skin and seed left behind.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium high heat until a drop of sauce sizzles sharply, about 350°F (175°C), and pour in the strained sauce all at once.
Stir as it splutters, then lower the heat and simmer 15 to 30 minutes, adding more soaking water as needed, until it darkens and lightly coats a spoon; season with salt.
Use it warm for enchiladas, chilaquiles, tamales or pozole rojo. It keeps 5 days in the refrigerator or 3 months frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the dried chiles and tomato.

citations.source: Mexican Food Journal, Guajillo Chile Salsa
Maricruz Avalos, Chile Guajillo Sauce

recipes.curationNote: Mexican Food Journal's technique (chiles simmered 1 minute and soaked 15, blended with soaking water, strained, fried in oil and simmered until thick and darker) joined with Maricruz Avalos's tomato, onion, cumin and oregano, which is the cooked version used for enchiladas and pozole rojo. Chile count set between the two (16 and 10). Guajillo is not in the database, so the chiles are not counted in nutrients. About 3 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup (60 ml), 12 servings.

recipes.name: Salsa de Jitomate para Entomatadas
recipes.flavorProfile: A smooth, mellow tomato sauce, sweet from roasting and long cooking, with roasted garlic, a little serrano warmth and the herbal note of epazote.
recipes.healthBenefit: Cooked tomato is a good source of lycopene and vitamin C, and the sauce uses only a spoonful of fat.

components.note: 1 1/2 cups

ingredients.cutPrep: 1 small white onion, in thick slices

ingredients.prepNote: to taste, depending on the stock

instructions: Roast the tomatoes, onion slices, garlic and serranos on a hot comal or under a broiler, turning, until blackened in spots and soft, about 6 minutes per side for the tomatoes and less for the rest.
Let them cool, peel the garlic, and peel the tomatoes if you like a very smooth sauce.
Blend everything until smooth.
Heat the lard in a wide saucepan over medium high heat until a drop of purée sizzles sharply, about 350°F (175°C), then pour in the purée all at once.
Stir almost constantly for 5 to 7 minutes, until it darkens and thickens.
Add the stock and epazote and simmer gently 20 to 30 minutes, until it coats a tortilla lightly; take out the epazote and season with salt.
Dip warm tortillas in it for entomatadas. It keeps 4 days in the refrigerator or 3 months frozen.

citations.source: Rick Bayless, Entomatadas
Bea Orviz Tjiang, Entomatadas de pollo y queso, Directo al Paladar

recipes.curationNote: Rick Bayless's method (tomatoes, onion, garlic and serrano roasted, puréed, fried in lard until thick, then simmered with broth and epazote 20 to 30 minutes), with the tomato doubled to make enough for about 12 entomatadas. Directo al Paladar confirms the same base of tomato, onion, two garlic cloves and chicken broth blended smooth. No Mexican site's entomatada recipe could be opened (several returned 403). About 3 cups; one serving is 1/2 cup.

recipes.name: Adobo de Chiles Secos
recipes.flavorProfile: A thick, dark red paste, tangy with vinegar and deep with ancho, guajillo and pasilla, warm with clove, cinnamon and cumin.
recipes.healthBenefit: Dried chiles carry carotenoids and the paste has almost no fat, so it flavors meat heavily for very little added energy.

ingredients.cutPrep: half a white onion, in pieces

ingredients.prepNote: apple cider or a mild white vinegar
plus hot water to soak the chiles, discarded

instructions: Toast the chiles on a medium hot comal a few seconds per side, pressing them flat, until fragrant and lightly blistered but not dark, which makes them bitter.
Cover them with very hot water and soak 20 to 30 minutes until soft, then drain.
In the same dry pan over medium low heat, toast the cloves and canela 30 to 60 seconds until they smell, and take them out before they darken.
Roast the onion and unpeeled garlic in the pan, turning, until soft and charred in spots, 8 to 10 minutes; peel the garlic.
Blend the chiles, spices, onion, garlic, cumin, pepper, oregano, vinegar, salt and the 120 ml water until completely smooth and thick, adding a little more water only if the blender stalls.
Rub it over meat and marinate 4 hours or overnight in the refrigerator before roasting, braising or grilling. The paste keeps a month in a closed jar in the refrigerator.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the ancho and pasilla chiles.

citations.source: Zahie Téllez, el truco para preparar el adobo perfecto, Directo al Paladar
Rick Bayless, Red Chile Adobo (Adobo de Chile Seco Estilo Nuevo)

recipes.curationNote: Mexican chef Zahie Téllez's adobo: 4 guajillo, 3 pasilla and 3 ancho, 3 or 4 cloves and half a cinnamon stick toasted lightly, half an onion and 2 garlic charred, blended with oregano, a little water and 1 cup vinegar. Spice amounts not given there come from Rick Bayless's adobo (cumin, black pepper, oregano, 1 1/2 teaspoons salt). Guajillo is not in the database and not counted in nutrients. About 2 1/2 cups; one serving is 2 tablespoons, 20 servings.

recipes.name: Recado Rojo (Achiote Paste)
recipes.flavorProfile: Earthy, peppery and lightly bitter, brick red achiote brightened by sour orange and warmed with cumin, allspice, clove and roasted garlic.
recipes.healthBenefit: Achiote seeds carry carotenoid pigments, and the paste is mostly spice and citrus, so it adds deep flavor with little fat.

ingredients.name: sour orange juice (naranja agria)
ingredients.prepNote: or 2 parts sweet orange juice to 1 part lime juice

instructions: Heat the lard in a skillet over medium high heat until nearly smoking and toast the achiote seeds about 5 minutes, shaking the pan constantly so they do not burn.
Tip the seeds into a heatproof bowl, pour the hot sour orange juice over them, and soak 3 to 4 hours at room temperature or overnight in the refrigerator, until soft.
Toast the cumin, peppercorns, allspice and cloves in a dry pan over medium heat 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant, then the oregano for a few seconds, each taken out before it darkens.
Roast the unpeeled garlic in the same pan, turning, 5 to 10 minutes until blackened in spots and soft, then peel it.
Blend the seeds with their juice, the spices, garlic and salt in batches until it forms a smooth, thick paste, adding a splash more juice only if needed.
Pack it into a jar and refrigerate for several weeks, or freeze in tablespoon portions. Thin it with more sour orange to marinate cochinita, pollo pibil or fish.

nutritionHighlights.note: Bixin and norbixin, the red pigments of achiote seed.

citations.source: Zarela Martínez, Achiote Paste (Pasta de achiote)
Grupo Animal, Rojo que te quiero rojo: qué es el achiote y cómo utilizarlo
Excélsior, Cómo hacer adobo para cochinita pibil

recipes.curationNote: Zarela Martínez's paste from whole seeds (1 cup achiote toasted in lard and soaked in 3 cups hot orange juice, cumin, peppercorns, oregano, roasted garlic, salt; keeps weeks). Grupo Animal describes the Yucatecan recaudo as seeds soaked for pigment and ground with oregano, clove, cumin and pepper, and Excélsior adds allspice and the sweet orange and lime stand in for sour orange, so allspice and clove were added and the liquid set as sour orange. Achiote and sour orange are not in the database and not counted in nutrients. About 3 cups; one serving is 1 tablespoon, 48 servings.

recipes.name: Mole Poblano
recipes.flavorProfile: Thick, glossy and dark reddish brown, layering the fruity heat of mulato, ancho and pasilla chiles with toasted sesame, almond and peanut, sweet raisin and plantain notes, warm spice and a quiet bitterness of chocolate.
recipes.healthBenefit: Dried chiles bring carotenoids, and the sesame, almonds and peanuts add plant protein, magnesium and vitamin E, so a small serving carries a good deal of nourishment.

components.note: two day old tortillas, fried crisp as a thickener
one day old roll, sliced and fried
about 1 L, added a little at a time

ingredients.cutPrep: 6 dried anchos, stemmed, seeded and deveined
4 dried pasillas, stemmed, seeded and deveined

ingredients.prepNote: a spoonful kept back for garnish

ingredients.cutPrep: half a white onion, thickly sliced

ingredients.name: Mexican table chocolate
ingredients.prepNote: chocolate de mesa, ground cacao with sugar and canela
for frying the chiles, seeds and bread and then the sauce
to taste, to round off the chiles
hot, for soaking the chiles; part of it blended in

instructions: Heat 2 tbsp of the lard in a heavy skillet over medium heat and fry the chiles a few at a time, 10 to 20 seconds per side, just until they puff and smell toasty; pull them before they blacken or the mole turns bitter.
Cover the fried chiles with the hot water and soak 20 to 30 minutes, until soft.
Meanwhile roast the tomatoes, tomatillos, onion and garlic on a dry comal over medium heat, turning, 10 to 15 minutes, until blistered and soft; peel the garlic.

Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium low heat, stirring, 2 to 3 minutes, until golden. Toast the canela, cloves, allspice, peppercorns, anise and cumin together for 30 to 60 seconds, until fragrant.

In a little more lard, fry the almonds and peanuts 2 to 3 minutes until golden, then the raisins about 30 seconds until they puff, then the tortillas and bread until browned and crisp, lifting each out as it is done.

Blend in separate batches so each grinds smooth: the drained chiles with about 2 cups of the soaking water; the roasted vegetables; then the seeds, nuts, raisins, spices, tortillas and bread with 1 to 2 cups of the caldo. Blend each 2 to 3 minutes, until very smooth.

Heat the remaining lard in a wide heavy pot over medium high heat until a drop of chile purée sizzles sharply, about 350°F (175°C). Pour in the chile purée, stir as it splutters and fry 8 to 10 minutes, until thick and darker.
Add the vegetable purée and fry 5 minutes more, then the seed and nut paste, stirring constantly and scraping the bottom, another 5 to 10 minutes.

Stir in the rest of the caldo a little at a time, add the chocolate, sugar and salt, and simmer over low heat, uncovered and stirring often, 30 to 40 minutes, until glossy, thick enough to coat a spoon and with a sheen of fat on top.
Serve over poached turkey or chicken with the reserved sesame on top. It keeps 1 week in the refrigerator or 6 months frozen, and the flavour is better the next day.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the almonds, peanuts and sesame.
From the seeds, nuts and dried chiles.

citations.source: TV Azteca, MasterChef México: Mole poblano de Isabel Carvajal
Directo al Paladar, Bea Orviz Tjiang: Mole poblano

recipes.curationNote: Quantities follow Isabel Carvajal (6 mulato, 6 ancho, 4 pasilla, 50 g each of sesame, almond and peanut, 30 g raisin, 30 g chocolate, 1 L broth, fried in lard, blended in batches, cooked 30 to 40 minutes). Bea Orviz Tjiang gave the same chile trio, bread and tortilla, and the second simmer once the chocolate is in. Mulato and Mexican table chocolate are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 6 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup (about 60 g), 24 servings, so 8 servings is about 500 g.

recipes.name: Mole Negro Oaxaqueño
recipes.flavorProfile: Nearly black, thick and smooth, with deep smoky bitterness from chiles and seeds toasted almost to charcoal, balanced by plantain, raisin, Oaxacan chocolate and sugar, and an anise note from avocado leaves.
recipes.healthBenefit: A dense sauce of dried chiles, nuts and seeds that brings carotenoids, magnesium and vitamin E, eaten a little at a time.

components.note: toasted until black
one day old, torn and fried
about 1.7 L

ingredients.name: dried chilhuacle negro chiles
ingredients.prepNote: about 6 chiles; more mulato or pasilla where there are none

ingredients.cutPrep: about 10 dried pasilla negro chiles, stemmed and seeded, seeds kept
half a very ripe plantain, peeled and sliced
a 1 inch piece of Mexican canela

ingredients.name: Oaxacan chocolate
ingredients.prepNote: chocolate de mesa ground with sugar, almonds and canela

ingredients.name: avocado leaves
ingredients.prepNote: or 1/2 tsp anise seed where there are none
hot, for soaking the chiles; part of it blended in

instructions: Open a window or work outdoors. Toast the chiles a handful at a time on a comal over medium heat, pressing and turning, until they are black but not ash, 8 to 12 minutes per batch for the thick mulatos and less for the others. Soak them in the hot water 30 to 45 minutes, stirring now and then.

Toast 1/4 cup of the chile seeds in a dry skillet over medium heat, shaking, until black, 10 to 15 minutes; then set them alight with a match and let them burn out, cover with cold water and soak 10 minutes, and drain. This charred seed is what makes the mole black.

Roast the onion, garlic, tomato and tomatillos on the comal until blackened in spots and soft, 10 to 15 minutes; peel the garlic. Toast the sesame in a dry pan until golden, 2 to 3 minutes, and toast the tortilla over the flame until black.

Heat a little of the lard in a skillet over medium heat and fry, one at a time and lifting each out: the almonds and peanuts 2 to 3 minutes until browned, the plantain 3 to 4 minutes until deep brown, the raisins about 30 seconds until puffed, and the bread until golden.

Blend the drained chiles and seeds with 2 to 3 cups of the soaking water until completely smooth, 2 to 3 minutes, and strain. Separately blend the roasted vegetables, nuts, sesame, plantain, raisins, bread, tortilla and spices with 2 cups of the caldo until smooth, 2 to 3 minutes.

Heat the remaining lard in a large heavy pot over medium high heat until a drop of purée sizzles sharply, about 350°F (175°C). Add the chile purée and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, 8 to 12 minutes, until it is the colour of dark chocolate and very thick.
Add the nut and fruit purée and keep stirring and scraping, about 10 minutes more, until thick and shiny again.

Stir in the rest of the caldo, the chocolate, the toasted avocado leaves, the sugar and the salt. Simmer over medium low heat, partly covered and stirring often, 1 1/2 to 2 hours, until it coats a spoon thickly. Remove the leaves and adjust the salt and sugar.
Serve over turkey or chicken, or use it in tamales oaxaqueños and enmoladas. It keeps 1 week in the refrigerator or 6 months frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the almonds, peanuts and sesame.
From the seeds, nuts and chiles.
From the plantain, raisins and chiles.

citations.source: Rick Bayless, Oaxacan Black Mole
El Universal, Menú: Mole negro, receta tradicional oaxaqueña (Mulli Oaxaca)

recipes.curationNote: Quantities follow Rick Bayless (5 oz mulato, 1.5 oz chilhuacle, 3 oz pasilla negro, burned chile seeds, about 7 cups broth, simmered a couple of hours, 2.5 to 3 quarts). The El Universal recipe from Mulli Oaxaca confirmed the chilhuacle, mulato and pasilla mix, the plantain, bread and tortilla, avocado leaves, Oaxacan chocolate and lard. Mulato, chilhuacle, Oaxacan chocolate and avocado leaves are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 11 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup (about 60 g), 44 servings, so 8 servings is about 500 g.

recipes.name: Mole Coloradito
recipes.flavorProfile: Brick red and velvety, sweeter and lighter than mole negro, with ancho fruitiness, roasted tomato, sesame, a little plantain and a clear taste of Oaxacan chocolate and canela.
recipes.healthBenefit: Ancho chiles and roasted tomato bring carotenoids and vitamin C, and sesame adds calcium and healthy fats.

components.note: about 720 ml, part of it for soaking the chiles

ingredients.cutPrep: about 10 dried anchos, stemmed, seeded and deveined

ingredients.name: dried chilcostle chiles
ingredients.prepNote: about 50 g; guajillo where there are none

ingredients.cutPrep: half a white onion, thickly sliced

instructions: Toast the anchos and chilcostles on a comal over medium low heat, a few seconds per side, until fragrant and pliable; do not let them darken. Cover with 2 cups of hot caldo and soak 20 to 30 minutes, until soft.

Roast the tomatoes, onion and garlic on the comal over medium heat, turning, 10 to 15 minutes, until blistered and soft; peel the garlic. Toast the sesame in a dry pan, stirring, 2 to 3 minutes until golden, and the canela, cloves and allspice for 30 to 60 seconds.
Heat a spoonful of the lard and fry the plantain 3 to 4 minutes until browned, then the bread until golden.
Blend the chiles with their soaking caldo, the roasted vegetables, sesame, spices, oregano, plantain and bread until very smooth, 2 to 3 minutes, in two batches if needed. Strain for a silkier sauce.

Heat the remaining lard in a heavy pot over medium high heat until a drop of the paste sizzles sharply, about 350°F (175°C). Pour in the paste and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, 10 to 15 minutes, until thick, darker and starting to look curdled at the edges, what Oaxacan cooks call chinito.
Stir in the chocolate until it melts, then the remaining caldo, the sugar and salt. Simmer over low heat, stirring often, 25 to 35 minutes, until glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Serve over chicken or pork, or use it for enmoladas and tamales. It keeps 1 week in the refrigerator or 6 months frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the ancho chiles and tomato.

citations.source: México Desconocido: Receta de pollo en mole coloradito
Grupo Animal, Margarita Carrillo: El coloradito de Cocina de Piedra

recipes.curationNote: Ingredients follow México Desconocido (ancho, chilcoxle, roasted tomato, sesame, plantain, pan de yema, cloves, allspice, oregano, lard, chocolate), cut to half. Margarita Carrillo gave the chiles rehydrated in broth, 500 g roasted tomato, 90 g chocolate with canela, and the paste fried until chinito before simmering about 30 minutes until glossy. Chilcostle, pan de yema and Oaxacan chocolate are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 6 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup (about 60 g), 24 servings.

recipes.name: Mole Amarillo
recipes.flavorProfile: Orange yellow, light and brothy for a mole, with the mild fruit of guajillo or chilcostle, tart tomatillo, cumin and clove, thickened with masa and finished with the anise and pepper scent of hoja santa.
recipes.healthBenefit: A light mole with almost no fat, built on chiles, tomato and tomatillo that bring vitamin A and vitamin C, with masa for body.

components.note: about 125 g fresh masa, or 6 tbsp masa harina mixed with water
about 1 L, 1 cup of it blended with the masa

ingredients.name: dried guajillo chiles
ingredients.prepNote: about 6; in Oaxaca chilcostle or chile costeño amarillo

ingredients.cutPrep: about 6 tomatillos, husked, rinsed and halved
a quarter of a white onion

ingredients.name: hoja santa leaves
ingredients.prepNote: or 4 avocado leaves added with the broth
for simmering the chiles and tomatoes

instructions: Toast the chile pieces on a dry comal over medium heat, pressing with a spatula, until they crackle and change colour slightly, a few seconds per side.
Put the chiles in a saucepan with the tomatoes, tomatillos, onion, garlic and the water. Simmer, partly covered, over medium low heat 10 to 15 minutes, until everything is soft.
Grind the cloves, cinnamon, peppercorns and cumin and add them to a blender with the oregano and everything from the saucepan, liquid included. Blend until smooth, 1 to 2 minutes.

Heat the lard in the washed saucepan over medium heat until shimmering, set a strainer over the pot and press the purée through it into the hot fat. Stir 5 to 8 minutes, until it thickens enough to show the bottom of the pot with each stroke.
Stir in 3 1/2 cups of the caldo (and the avocado leaves if using them in place of hoja santa) and simmer over medium low heat 20 minutes.

Blend the masa with the remaining 1 cup of caldo until smooth and strain it into the simmering sauce, whisking constantly, 3 to 5 minutes, until the sauce lightens in colour, returns to a simmer and thickens to the texture of a light cream soup.

Tear in the hoja santa, simmer 1 to 2 minutes more and season with salt. Serve with chicken, beef or vegetables such as chayote and green beans, or use it for empanadas de amarillo. It keeps 4 days in the refrigerator; it thickens as it cools, so loosen it with caldo.

citations.source: My Slice of Mexico: Oaxaca style yellow mole (mole amarillo de Oaxaca)
Rick Bayless, Chicken Breasts with Yellow Mole and Roasted Vegetables

recipes.curationNote: Ingredients follow Irene of My Slice of Mexico (45 g light chiles, 350 g each tomato and tomatillo, cinnamon, clove, pepper, oregano, cumin, masa slurry, hoja santa, lard), trimmed slightly; method follows Rick Bayless (chiles simmered with the tomato and tomatillo 15 minutes, strained into hot fat, 3 1/2 cups broth simmered 20 minutes, then masa blended with 1 cup broth). Guajillo and hoja santa are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 5 cups; one serving is 1/2 cup, 10 servings, because this thin mole is eaten more like a stew than a thick paste.

recipes.name: Mole Verde
recipes.flavorProfile: Pale green and creamy, nutty from toasted pumpkin seed and peanut, tart with tomatillo, hot with serrano, and bright with fresh cilantro, epazote, lettuce, spinach and hoja santa added near the end.
recipes.healthBenefit: Pumpkin seeds bring magnesium, zinc and iron, and the raw greens and tomatillo add folate, vitamin K and vitamin C.

components.note: about 2 L, half blended with the seeds and half with the vegetables

ingredients.cutPrep: a quarter of a white onion

instructions: Toast the pepitas in a dry skillet over medium low heat, stirring constantly, 3 to 5 minutes, until they puff and start to pop but stay green; then toast the peanuts 3 to 4 minutes until golden. Let them cool.
Roast the tomatillos, serranos, onion and garlic on a comal over medium heat, turning, 8 to 12 minutes, until softened and spotted brown.
Grind the pepitas and peanuts dry in two batches, then blend them with 1 L of the caldo until smooth, 2 to 3 minutes.

Blend the roasted tomatillos, chiles, onion and garlic with the other 1 L of caldo until smooth. Separately blend the cilantro, epazote, lettuce, spinach and hoja santa with a ladle of this purée until bright green and fine, and set that aside.
Heat the lard in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the seed purée and the tomatillo purée and cook, stirring constantly so the seeds do not catch or curdle, 15 minutes, keeping it at a bare simmer.
Stir in the herb purée, season with salt and pepper and cook 4 to 5 minutes more, just until heated through, so the green stays fresh. A hard boil splits the seed sauce and dulls the colour.
Serve with pork, chicken or vegetables, with rice, beans and tortillas. It keeps 3 days in the refrigerator; reheat gently and loosen with caldo.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the pumpkin seeds and peanuts.
From the cilantro, lettuce and spinach.

citations.source: Cookpad México, Lilia: Mole verde
Zarela Martínez, Mole Verde (Green Mole)

recipes.curationNote: Ingredients and quantities follow Lilia on Cookpad México, the pumpkin seed and peanut mole verde of Puebla and central Mexico (1 1/2 cups pepita, 1/2 cup peanut, 2 L broth, 400 g tomatillo, 4 serranos, cilantro, epazote, lettuce, spinach, radish leaves or hoja santa, lard, 20 minutes). Zarela Martínez supplied the step of blending the raw herbs separately and adding them for the last 4 to 5 minutes to keep the colour; her Oaxacan mole verde is thickened with masa instead of seeds. Hoja santa is not in the database, so it is not counted in nutrients. About 10 cups; one serving is 1/2 cup, 20 servings.

recipes.name: Pipián Verde
recipes.flavorProfile: Thick, nutty and grassy, almost all pumpkin seed and sesame ground with tart tomatillo, serrano heat, scallion and a big handful of cilantro, parsley, epazote and radish leaves, cooked until small pools of oil rise.
recipes.healthBenefit: Pumpkin and sesame seeds carry magnesium, zinc, iron and calcium, and the cooked greens and tomatillo add folate and vitamin K.

components.note: about 720 ml

ingredients.baseName: Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb)
ingredients.cutPrep: 3 scallions, white and light green parts, chopped
1 packed cup leaves and upper stems

ingredients.prepNote: to cover the tomatillos; 1 cup of it blended in

instructions: Cover the tomatillos, garlic and chiles with the water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer over medium high heat and cook about 10 minutes, until the tomatillos turn from bright to dull green and are soft but still whole.
Toast the pepitas in a dry skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly, 3 to 5 minutes, until lightly browned and popping; then toast the sesame 1 to 2 minutes until golden.

Grind the pepitas in a blender until fine, add the sesame and grind again. Add the tomatillos, garlic and chiles, 1 cup of their cooking water, the scallions, cilantro, parsley, epazote, lettuce, radish leaves and salt, and blend until completely smooth, 2 to 3 minutes.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium high heat, pour in the purée with the caldo and stir well.

When it simmers, lower the heat to medium and cook, partly covered and stirring often, 25 to 30 minutes, until it coats the back of a wooden spoon and has broken, with small pools of oil on the surface.
Serve with chicken, pork or calabacitas, or use it for enchiladas. It keeps 3 days in the refrigerator and thickens as it cools; loosen it with caldo.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the pumpkin and sesame seeds.

citations.source: Pati Jinich, Pipián verde con verduras
Cookpad México, Edgar Alberto Ortiz Tirado: Pipián verde súper rápido

recipes.curationNote: Quantities and method follow Pati Jinich (1 lb tomatillo boiled 10 minutes, 1 1/3 cups pepita, 1/3 cup sesame, scallion, cilantro, parsley, epazote, radish leaves, 3 cups broth, cooked about 30 minutes until it breaks). Edgar Ortiz Tirado of Mexico City added the lettuce and a short boil. Unlike the mole verde in this collection, pipián has no peanut and leans on the seeds alone. Radish leaves are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 6 cups; one serving is 1/2 cup, 12 servings.

recipes.name: Cebolla Morada Encurtida
recipes.flavorProfile: Bright pink, crisp and sharply sour from naranja agria, with a slow habanero heat and a light note of allspice and bay.
recipes.healthBenefit: Raw red onion keeps its quercetin and other flavonoids, and the citrus brings vitamin C, all with no oil or sugar.

ingredients.cutPrep: 1 large red onion, sliced very thin into half moons

ingredients.name: sour orange juice (naranja agria)
ingredients.prepNote: or 160 ml lime juice with 80 ml orange juice

ingredients.name: habanero chile
ingredients.cutPrep: charred, then slit or sliced into rings
ingredients.prepNote: or a charred jalapeño for less heat
about 1 1/2 tsp, part of it rubbed into the onion

instructions: Toss the sliced onion with the salt in a bowl and press it gently with your fingertips for 1 to 2 minutes, until it softens and starts to weep.

Char the habanero on a dry comal over medium heat, turning a couple of times, 3 to 6 minutes, until the skin is blistered in spots. Slit it, or slice it into rings for more heat; wear gloves or wash your hands well afterwards.
Mix the sour orange juice with the allspice and pepper, pour it over the onion, add the bay leaves and the habanero and stir.
Leave at room temperature 30 minutes to 2 hours, stirring once or twice, until the onion turns bright pink and softens.
Serve with cochinita pibil, panuchos, salbutes, poc chuc and tacos. Keep covered in a glass jar in the refrigerator up to 1 week.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the sour orange juice and onion.

citations.source: Larousse Cocina, Ricardo Muñoz Zurita: Cebolla curada
Pati Jinich: Cebollas encurtidas yucatecas

recipes.curationNote: Ricardo Muñoz Zurita gave the Yucatecan method of rubbing the onion with salt before the sour orange juice and resting 30 minutes. Pati Jinich gave the quantities (1 cup juice, 1 large red onion, black pepper, allspice, bay, salt) and the charred chile with a rest of 30 minutes to 2 hours; she uses jalapeño, and habanero follows the Yucatecan table the base list asks for. Red onion is entered as Veg Onion, the same food in another colour. Sour orange and habanero are not in the database, so they are not counted in nutrients. About 2 cups; one serving is 2 tbsp, 16 servings.

recipes.name: Chiles en Escabeche
recipes.flavorProfile: Olive green jalapeño strips, sweet carrot coins and soft onion and garlic in a sharp vinegar brine scented with bay, thyme, marjoram and Mexican oregano.
recipes.healthBenefit: Jalapeños and carrots carry vitamin C and beta carotene, and a vinegar pickle keeps them on hand with little fat and no sugar to speak of.

ingredients.cutPrep: stemmed, cut lengthwise in strips; seeds and veins out for less heat
2 to 3 carrots, peeled and sliced 1/4 cm on the diagonal
half a large white onion in thin strips
6 to 8 cloves, peeled and left whole

instructions: Toss the jalapeños, carrots and onion with the salt in a large bowl and leave 1 hour, then drain, keeping the juices they release.
Heat the oil in a wide, deep pot over medium low heat. Add the carrots and stir 4 to 5 minutes to coat and soften them without browning.
Add the onion, garlic and jalapeños and cook, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes, until the kitchen smells of chile and the vegetables are just starting to soften.
Pour in the vinegar, the water and the reserved juices, add the bay, thyme, marjoram, oregano, peppercorns, cloves, cumin and sugar, and bring to a slow boil over medium heat.
Boil 2 to 5 minutes, until the jalapeños turn from bright green to a dull olive green, then turn off the heat and let everything cool in the pot.
Pack into clean glass jars, covering the vegetables with the brine, and refrigerate at least 1 day before eating. They keep up to 3 months refrigerated with the lid kept on.

citations.source: Los Originarios: Chiles jalapeños en escabeche
Pati Jinich: Amo los jalapeños en escabeche
Cookpad México, Afrodita Fiallos: Mi receta especial de chiles jalapeños en escabeche

recipes.curationNote: Ingredients follow Los Originarios, halved (1 kg jalapeños, 3 to 4 carrots, half a large onion, a head of garlic, 1/2 cup oil, 5 bay leaves, thyme, marjoram, Mexican oregano, white vinegar to cover, brought to a slow boil until olive green). Pati Jinich gave the hour of salting, the water in the brine and the peppercorn, clove, cumin and sugar. Afrodita Fiallos confirmed vinegar and water together and the overnight rest. About 4 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup, 16 servings.

recipes.name: Crema Mexicana
recipes.flavorProfile: Thick but pourable, rich and mildly tangy, lighter in sourness than sour cream, with a little salt and lime.
recipes.healthBenefit: Culturing the cream with buttermilk adds live lactic bacteria, and a spoonful brings vitamin A along with its fat.

ingredients.cutPrep: 36% milk fat or higher, pasteurized but not ultra pasteurized

instructions: Warm the cream in a saucepan over low heat 1 to 2 minutes, just to room temperature, about 70°F (21°C); it should not feel warm to the touch.
Stir in the buttermilk gently until even and pour into a clean glass jar.
Cover loosely with a cloth or a loose lid and leave undisturbed at room temperature, away from sunlight, 12 to 24 hours, until it has thickened like yogurt. Keep it below 100°F (38°C) the whole time.
Whisk in the salt and lime juice just until smooth.

Close the jar and refrigerate at least 2 hours, best overnight, as it keeps thickening. Use it on enchiladas, tostadas, elotes, sopes and soups. It keeps up to 2 weeks refrigerated and should not be frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the cultured buttermilk, when it is not heated afterwards.

citations.source: Villa Cocina, Rossana Figueroa: Crema Mexicana
Mexican Please: Homemade Mexican Crema

recipes.curationNote: Quantities follow Rossana Figueroa of Villa Cocina (2 cups cream at 36% fat or more, 1/2 cup cultured buttermilk, 1/2 tsp salt, 24 hours at room temperature, then chilled). Mexican Please gave the step of warming the cream to room temperature first, the 12 to 24 hour range and the lime. About 2 1/2 cups; one serving is 2 tbsp (30 ml), 20 servings.

recipes.name: Queso Fresco
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft, moist and crumbly, milky and lightly salty, with no sourness; it softens with heat but does not melt into strings.
recipes.healthBenefit: A fresh cheese that brings protein, calcium and vitamin B12 from whole milk with only salt added.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.name: rennet (cuajo)
ingredients.cutPrep: liquid, or about 1/8 of a rennet tablet crushed
ingredients.prepNote: check the label for the dose; the strength varies by brand
2 tbsp to dissolve the rennet and about 140 ml added to the curd

instructions: Warm the milk in a large pot over low heat, stirring, to 95°F (35°C), about 10 to 15 minutes. Do not let it go above 100°F (38°C).

Dissolve the rennet in 2 tbsp of cool water, stir it into the milk for 2 to 3 minutes, then cover and leave off the heat 25 to 45 minutes, until the milk sets like a soft gelatin and a knife lifts a clean break.
Cut the curd into a rough grid with a long knife, add the remaining water and leave 15 minutes. Break the curd into small pieces with a spoon and leave another 15 minutes as the whey separates.
