Ladle off the whey, then pour the curd into a cheesecloth lined colander and squeeze out the whey by hand until what runs out turns from yellowish to white.
Knead the curd in a bowl about 10 minutes with the salt, tasting and adding more if needed.

Pack the curd firmly into a round mould or a basket lined with cloth, press it down with your hands and put a weight on top. Leave 2 hours in the refrigerator, or overnight for a firmer cheese, then unmould.
Keep wrapped in the refrigerator and eat within 5 to 7 days. Crumble it over beans, enchiladas, esquites, sopes and soups. About 650 g.

citations.source: Cookpad México, Sofia Carolina Castillo Villafuerte (Aldama, Tamaulipas): Queso fresco
Cuajo para Queso: Cómo hacer queso fresco con cuajo

recipes.curationNote: Sofia Castillo Villafuerte of Tamaulipas gave the ranch method (rennet from the vet supply, curd cut with a spoon, pressed by hand, salted and packed into a lined mould; 5 L gave about 860 g). Cuajo para Queso gave the temperature of 35°C, the 25 minute set, the added water, the 15 minute rests and kneading with salt before a 2 hour press. Milk set at 4 L. Rennet is not in the database and adds nothing measurable. Most of the whey runs off, so the cheese carries far less than the full milk: about 650 g; one serving is 30 g, 21 servings.

recipes.name: Chorizo Mexicano
recipes.flavorProfile: Loose, brick red and juicy when fried, tangy with vinegar, earthy with ancho and guajillo, and warm with cumin, clove, oregano and garlic.
recipes.healthBenefit: Made at home it is pork, chiles, vinegar and spices with no fillers, nitrites or colouring, and the chiles bring carotenoids.

ingredients.cutPrep: coarsely ground, from leg and loin or shoulder
about 6 dried anchos, stemmed, seeded and deveined

ingredients.prepNote: hot, for soaking the chiles only; not blended in

instructions: Wipe the chiles with a damp cloth and toast them on a comal over medium heat a few seconds per side, until fragrant. Cover with the hot water and soak 15 to 30 minutes, until soft.
Grind the cumin, peppercorns, oregano, marjoram, thyme, cloves, allspice, coriander and bay to a powder in a mortar or spice grinder.
Drain the chiles, discarding the soaking water, and blend them with the vinegar, garlic, paprika, ground spices and salt into a thick, very smooth paste, 1 to 2 minutes.
In a large glass bowl, mix the pork and fat with the chile paste with gloved hands until evenly red, 3 to 5 minutes.
Cover and refrigerate 24 hours so the vinegar and spices season the meat. For a drier chorizo, set it in a covered strainer over a bowl in the refrigerator another 12 to 24 hours to drain.
Divide into 100 g portions and wrap, or stuff into soaked casings and tie every 10 to 15 cm. It keeps 5 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen raw.

To cook, fry it loose in a skillet over medium heat with a teaspoon of oil, breaking it up, 8 to 12 minutes, until it is browned and cooked through to 160°F (71°C). Use it with eggs, potatoes, beans, queso fundido or tacos.

nutritionHighlights.note: Pork is one of the richest sources of vitamin B1.
From the dried chiles and paprika.

citations.source: Los Originarios: Chorizo de cerdo casero
El Diario NY: Cómo hacer chorizo fresco mexicano

recipes.curationNote: Meat, chiles, garlic, vinegar and the 24 hour rest plus 12 to 24 hour drain follow Los Originarios (1 kg pork, about 75 g ancho, 50 g guajillo, 6 to 8 garlic, 1/2 cup cider vinegar). El Diario gave the 170 g of pork fat, the paprika and the fuller spice list (coriander, marjoram, thyme, cloves, allspice, bay); its 1 cup vinegar and 2 tbsp salt were brought down part way. Guajillo is not in the database, so it is not counted in nutrients. About 1.2 kg raw; one serving is 100 g, 12 servings, so 2 servings is about 200 g.

recipes.name: Cajeta
recipes.flavorProfile: Glossy, deep amber caramel with the faint tang of goat milk, a long cooked milk sweetness and a hint of canela.
recipes.healthBenefit: A sweet to enjoy in small amounts; goat milk brings some calcium and protein to it.

ingredients.cutPrep: goat milk, 250 ml of it kept back

instructions: In a heavy pot that holds at least 4 L (the milk foams up), stir 1 1/4 L of the goat milk with the sugar and canela until the sugar dissolves before turning on the heat.
Bring to a boil over medium low heat. Whisk in the cornstarch dissolved in the water and simmer 10 minutes, stirring.
Take the pot off the heat, dissolve the baking soda in the reserved 250 ml milk and stir it in; it foams, which is why the pot must be large. Return to the heat.
Simmer over low to medium low heat, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, 45 minutes to 1 hour, until it turns golden and starts to thicken.

From then on stir constantly, scraping the bottom, another 20 to 40 minutes, until it is deep amber and a spoon drawn across the bottom leaves the pot clear for a moment; a drop on a cold plate should hold its shape. On a thermometer this is about 220°F to 225°F (104°C to 107°C).

Take out the canela and pour the cajeta into clean glass jars while hot; it thickens as it cools. Cool before closing and keep refrigerated up to 2 months. Warm it gently to loosen it for crepas, churros or fruit.

citations.source: México Desconocido: Receta de cajeta de Celaya
Infobae México: Receta de cajeta de Celaya

recipes.curationNote: Quantities follow Infobae (1 1/2 L goat milk with 1/4 L of it kept back to dissolve the baking soda, a little starch in water, a 5 cm cinnamon stick, simmered until the bottom of the pot shows) with the sugar set between its 250 g and México Desconocido's 1 3/4 cups per litre. México Desconocido gave the thick, roomy pot and the stirring that turns constant once it thickens; its corn syrup was left out. The only goat milk row in the database is long life goat milk, which is the same milk heat treated. About 2 1/4 cups; one serving is 2 tbsp, 18 servings.

recipes.name: Miel de Piloncillo
recipes.flavorProfile: Dark, pourable syrup tasting of molasses and caramel from the unrefined cane sugar, warmed with canela, a little anise and clove and a strip of orange peel.
recipes.healthBenefit: A sweetener to use sparingly; piloncillo keeps some of the cane minerals, such as potassium and iron, that white sugar loses.

ingredients.name: orange peel
ingredients.cutPrep: a strip of the coloured zest only, no white pith

instructions: Put the piloncillo in a small pot with the hot water, canela, anise, cloves and orange peel and leave a few minutes to start dissolving, breaking up the pieces with a spoon.
Bring to a boil over medium heat, then simmer, stirring now and then, 15 to 20 minutes, until it has reduced to about 2 cups and looks like a light syrup that coats a spoon, about 220°F (104°C).
Take out the canela, cloves and peel, and strain it if any bits of cane remain.
Serve it warm over buñuelos, capirotada, churros or hot cakes, or use it to sweeten café de olla. It thickens as it cools; keep it in a jar in the refrigerator up to 2 weeks.

citations.source: Pati Jinich: Buñuelos, valen la pena
Gastrolab: Miel con piloncillo para churros y buñuelos
Cocina Vital: Miel de piloncillo y canela espesa

recipes.curationNote: Pati Jinich gave piloncillo, hot water and a cinnamon stick simmered about 15 minutes to a syrup, then strained (500 g to 1 cup water, a thick syrup). Gastrolab gave the thinner ratio of 200 g to 1 cup water with clove, anise and orange peel, and Cocina Vital the pinch of anise. Set between them at 300 g to 2 cups water for a pourable syrup. About 2 cups; one serving is 1/4 cup, 8 servings.
